title: Non Parametric Tests, Correlation, and Regression

steps.title: When parametric tests fail
steps.tx: **Non parametric tests** drop the normality assumption by analysing ranks instead of raw values, suiting skewed data, ordinal scales, small samples, and outliers that would poison means. They sacrifice some power when data truly are normal (about five percent efficiency loss for the classic rank tests), a small insurance premium most field datasets should gladly pay.
steps.say: Rank tests trade a little power for freedom from normality. Skewed, ordinal, or tiny data demand them.

steps.title: Mann Whitney U test
steps.tx: The **Mann Whitney U test** (Wilcoxon rank sum) is the non parametric twin of the unpaired t test: pool both groups, rank all values, and compare rank sums; if groups match, ranks intermingle evenly. It compares distributions (often summarised as medians) for two independent groups: hospital stay by sex, antibody titres by vaccination status, pain scores by analgesia arm.
steps.say: Mann Whitney ranks both groups together and compares rank sums. It is the unpaired t test without normality.

nodes.label: Pool both groups, rank all values

steps.title: Wilcoxon signed rank test
steps.tx: For paired data the **Wilcoxon signed rank test** ranks the absolute within pair differences and restores their signs, testing whether positive and negative ranks balance: the non parametric twin of the paired t test. It suits before after pain scores, skewed biochemical changes, and small paired samples where difference normality cannot be trusted.
steps.say: Signed rank is the paired twin: rank the changes, keep their signs, test the balance.

steps.title: Kruskal Wallis test
steps.tx: Extending ranks to three or more independent groups gives the **Kruskal Wallis test**, the non parametric ANOVA: rank everything, compare average ranks per group with an H statistic judged on chi square. A significant result needs post hoc pairwise rank tests with correction. Typical uses compare ordinal scores or skewed costs across three treatment arms or districts.
steps.say: Kruskal Wallis is ANOVA on ranks for three or more groups. Follow significance with corrected pairwise tests.

steps.title: Correlation: strength of association
steps.tx: **Correlation** quantifies linear association between two continuous variables (height with weight, dose with response) without claiming causation. The scatter plot comes first: correlation computed on a curved or outlier ridden cloud lies confidently. Correlation describes this sample's pattern; regression (two steps on) will weaponise it for prediction, and examiners separate the twins by asking which predicts (regression).
steps.say: Correlation measures linear association, never causation. Always look at the scatter before trusting the number.

left.title: Correlation asks
points: Symmetric: x with y equals y with x

right.title: Regression asks
points: What y follows from this x?

steps.tx: Points climbing from lower left to upper right display a **positive correlation** between two continuous measures, such as dose and response. The line drawn through the cloud is the regression fit used for prediction, not the correlation itself. Correlation only summarises how tightly the points follow a straight pattern in this sample. A curved cloud or a few extreme outliers can still yield a misleading coefficient, so the scatter is read before any number.
steps.say: Points climbing from lower left to upper right display a positive correlation between two continuous measures, such as dose and response. steps.title: Pearson versus Spearman coefficients
steps.tx: The **Pearson correlation coefficient (r)** measures linear association on raw values, needing near normal continuous data, while Spearman's rank coefficient repeats the calculation on ranks, tolerating skew, ordinal data, and outliers. Both span minus one to plus one: sign gives direction, absolute value gives strength (above zero point seven strong, zero point four to zero point seven moderate, below weak, by common teaching bands).
steps.say: Pearson uses values; Spearman uses ranks. Both run minus one to plus one for direction and strength.

steps.title: Coefficient of determination
steps.tx: Squaring Pearson's r gives the **coefficient of determination (r squared)**: the share of variation in y explained by x. An r of zero point eight (impressive sounding) explains only sixty four percent of variation, leaving a third to other causes. This deflation is the honest antidote to correlation hype in abstracts and the press, and examinations test the squaring explicitly.
steps.say: Square r before celebrating. Zero point eight explains only sixty four percent of the variation.

steps.title: Simple linear regression
steps.tx: **Simple linear regression** fits y equals a plus b x by least squares: intercept a is the predicted y at x zero, slope b is the change in y per unit x (regression coefficient). The line predicts within the observed x range; extrapolation beyond it (adult doses to neonates by line extension) is the classic abuse. Residual scatter around the line grades the fit honestly.
steps.say: Regression draws the prediction line: intercept plus slope times x. Never extrapolate beyond observed data.

steps.title: Correlation traps that cost marks
steps.tx: Closing traps for **correlation and regression questions**: correlation never proves causation (confounding lurks), range restriction shrinks r, one outlier can invent or destroy r, ecological correlations over group averages exceed individual ones, and regression to the mean makes extreme first measurements improve spontaneously (the placebo free explanation of many before after claims). Each trap has ended examination answers and journal claims alike.
steps.say: Association is not causation, outliers forge coefficients, and extreme values regress to the mean on remeasurement.
